passages.t: Corinth: Aquila, Priscilla and the tentmakers
passages.happening:
Paul leaves Athens and goes to Corinth (verse 1). There he finds a Jew named Aquila, from Pontus, who has recently come from Italy with his wife Priscilla, “because Claudius had ordered all the Jews to leave Rome” (verse 2). Paul goes to see them, and he stays and works with them, “because they were tentmakers by trade, just as he was” (verse 3).

Every Sabbath he reasons in the synagogue, trying to persuade Jews and Greeks alike (verse 4).
passages.hearers:
Corinth had been destroyed by Rome in 146 BC and lay mostly empty for a century, until Julius Caesar founded it again in 44 BC as a Roman colony. By Paul's day it was a busy, wealthy city, the seat of the Roman governor of Achaia (southern Greece), with two harbours, one on each side of a narrow neck of land. It was new, mixed and eager for status.

Aquila came from Pontus, by the Black Sea, and he and Priscilla had been living in Rome. Why did they leave? The Roman writer Suetonius says the emperor Claudius expelled the Jews from Rome because they kept causing disturbances ‘at the prompting of Chrestus’. Most scholars think ‘Chrestus’ is a garbled form of ‘Christus’, Christ, and that the trouble in Rome's synagogues was over Jesus; some think Chrestus was a local troublemaker. The year usually given, about AD 49, comes from a much later writer and is disputed. Either way, Aquila and Priscilla were refugees.

They shared a trade with Paul. The word for ‘tentmaker’ may mean a maker of tents, or more broadly a worker in leather. It was hard work with the hands. Paul made a point of earning his own living so that he would not be a burden on the churches: “We worked night and day so that we would not be a burden to anyone while we proclaimed to you the gospel of God” (1 Thessalonians 2:9). A workshop opened on to the street, and as people came and went, there was time to talk.

Luke does not say whether Aquila and Priscilla were already believers when Paul met them. Many readers think they were, since nothing is said of their coming to faith.
passages.ot:
Work with the hands was honourable in Israel's Scriptures. The capable woman of Proverbs “works with eager hands” (Proverbs 31:13), and the Law sets work at the heart of the week: “Six days you shall labor and do all your work” (Exodus 20:9).

Refugees and strangers are near to God's heart in the Law: “Do not oppress a foreign resident, since you yourselves know how it feels to be foreigners” (Exodus 23:9). Paul, a travelling stranger, found a home with two people who had themselves been driven out of their city.
passages.asks: Paul paid his own way with a trade, and his workbench became a place to talk about Jesus. Ask how your daily work, whatever it is, could be a place of faithfulness and of honest conversation. And notice Aquila and Priscilla: driven out of their home, they opened it to someone else. Ask whom you could welcome.

passages.t: ‘Your blood be on your own heads’
passages.happening:
When Silas and Timothy come down from Macedonia, Paul gives himself fully to preaching, “testifying to the Jews that Jesus is the Christ” (verse 5). But when they oppose and insult him, he shakes out his garments and says, “Your blood be on your own heads! I am innocent of it. From now on I will go to the Gentiles” (verse 6).

So Paul leaves the synagogue and goes next door, to the house of Titus Justus, a worshipper of God (verse 7). “Crispus, the synagogue leader, and his whole household believed in the Lord. And many of the Corinthians who heard the message believed and were baptized” (verse 8).
passages.hearers:
Silas and Timothy probably brought a gift from the churches in Macedonia. Paul later reminded the Corinthians that ‘the brothers who came from Macedonia supplied my needs’ (2 Corinthians 11:9). So Paul could stop working for a time and give himself fully to preaching.

Who does Luke mean by ‘the Jews’ here? Not the Jewish people, and not even all the Jews of Corinth, since the leader of the synagogue himself, Crispus, believes with his whole household (verse 8). He means those in the synagogue at Corinth who opposed and insulted Paul. Paul, who answers them, is a Jew too. The note on Acts 2:22-28 explains how verses like this were later turned against the Jewish people, and why this site rejects that reading.

Paul's words sound harsh to modern ears, and they need to be read as his hearers would hear them. ‘Your blood be on your own heads’ is the language of the watchman in the prophet Ezekiel. God set Ezekiel as a watchman over Israel, whose task was to blow the trumpet when danger came. If he warned the people and they did not listen, the guilt was theirs, not his. Paul is saying: I have warned you, and I have done what God asked of me. ‘I am innocent of it.’ It is not a curse. It is a watchman laying down his responsibility. Shaking out his garments was a gesture that said the same: I am clear of this.

‘From now on I will go to the Gentiles’ is a turn in one city, Corinth, as it was at Pisidian Antioch (13:46). It is not a turn away from the Jewish people. In the very next town, Ephesus, Paul goes straight into the synagogue (verse 19). And he goes only next door. The house of Titus Justus, a Gentile who worshipped Israel's God, is beside the synagogue, and the leader of the synagogue follows him.
passages.ot:
God told Ezekiel, “if anyone hears the sound of the horn but fails to heed the warning, and the sword comes and takes him away, his blood will be on his own head” (Ezekiel 33:4). And to the watchman himself: “But if you warn a wicked man and he does not turn from his wickedness and his wicked way, he will die in his iniquity, but you will have saved yourself” (Ezekiel 3:19).

Shaking out a garment as a sign has an Old Testament example too. Nehemiah, after making the leaders promise to do justice, says, “I also shook out the folds of my robe” (Nehemiah 5:13), as a picture of what would happen to anyone who broke the promise.
passages.asks: Paul did what he was given to do, warned clearly, and then moved on, only as far as next door. Ask whether you carry guilt for other people's choices that is not yours to carry. And ask whether, when you are rejected, you go away bitter, or simply go next door and keep going.

passages.t: ‘Do not be afraid; keep on speaking’
passages.happening: One night the Lord speaks to Paul in a vision: “Do not be afraid; keep on speaking; do not be silent” (verse 9). “For I am with you and no one will lay a hand on you, because I have many people in this city” (verse 10). So Paul stays a year and a half, teaching the word of God among the Corinthians (verse 11).
passages.hearers:
Why would Paul need to hear ‘Do not be afraid’? Think of the last months. He had been beaten and jailed in Philippi, hunted out of Thessalonica and Berea, laughed at in Athens, and insulted in the synagogue at Corinth. He later wrote to the Corinthians, “I came to you in weakness and fear, and with much trembling” (1 Corinthians 2:3). The great apostle was afraid.

The Lord does not scold him. He gives three commands, keep speaking, do not be silent, do not be afraid, and two promises: I am with you, and no one will harm you here.

Then a surprising line: ‘I have many people in this city.’ Corinth was a proud and worldly port city. Most of its people did not yet believe. But the Lord already calls them his people. Paul is not trying to make God's people out of nothing. He is finding the people God already has.

So Paul stays a year and a half, his longest stay so far. Many think he wrote his first letter to the Thessalonians from here.
passages.ot:
The Lord's words echo what he said to his servants of old. To Joshua: “Do not be afraid; do not be discouraged, for the LORD your God is with you wherever you go” (Joshua 1:9). To Jeremiah: “Do not be afraid of them, for I am with you to deliver you” (Jeremiah 1:8). To Israel in exile: “Do not be afraid, for I am with you” (Isaiah 43:5).

And ‘I have many people in this city’ is like God's word to Elijah, who thought he was alone: “I have reserved seven thousand in Israel” (1 Kings 19:18).
passages.asks: Paul was afraid, and God met him with a promise, not a rebuke. If you are afraid to speak about your faith, ask whether you have heard the same words: ‘I am with you.’ And ask whom God may already be drawing in your town, your school or your workplace. You may be less alone than you think.

passages.happening:
While Gallio is proconsul of Achaia, “the Jews coordinated an attack on Paul and brought him before the judgment seat” (verse 12). They say, “This man is persuading the people to worship God in ways contrary to the law” (verse 13).

Before Paul can speak, Gallio tells them that if this were a matter of wrongdoing or a serious crime, he would hear them (verse 14). “But since it is a dispute about words and names and your own law, settle it yourselves. I refuse to be a judge of such things” (verse 15). He drives them away from the judgment seat (verse 16).

Then the crowd seizes Sosthenes, the leader of the synagogue, and beats him in front of the judgment seat, “But none of this was of concern to Gallio” (verse 17).
passages.hearers:
A proconsul was the governor of a Roman province. Gallio was the elder brother of the famous philosopher Seneca. A letter of the emperor Claudius, carved in stone at Delphi in Greece, names Gallio and allows his year of office to be fixed, most think in AD 51 to 52, some say 50 to 51. This is the surest fixed date in Paul's life, and the other dates of his travels are counted from it.

The ‘judgment seat’, in Greek the bema, was a raised stone platform in the city's main square from which officials gave judgment. A platform of this kind has been uncovered in the centre of the market square at Corinth.

‘The Jews’ here again means Paul's opponents in the synagogue at Corinth, not the Jewish people; the synagogue's leader had already believed (verse 8). The note on verses 5-8 above says more. Their charge is that Paul teaches people to worship God ‘contrary to the law’. They may mean their own law, the law of Moses, or Roman law.

Gallio's answer matters. To him this is an argument among Jews about words, names and their own law, not a crime. He will not take sides. That had large results. Many readers think a Roman governor had, in effect, treated the followers of Jesus as part of the Jewish community, not as a new and unlawful religion. For years afterwards, that gave Paul room to work.

Then an ugly scene. The crowd beats Sosthenes, the new leader of the synagogue, right in front of the governor, and Gallio does nothing. Luke does not say who did the beating or why. A man named Sosthenes is later with Paul when he writes to Corinth (1 Corinthians 1:1); some think he is the same man, but that is not certain.
passages.ot:
The Lord had promised Paul, ‘no one will lay a hand on you’, and he kept his word through a Roman governor who did not care about the dispute. The Old Testament often shows God at work through foreign rulers who do not know him, as with Cyrus of Persia: “I will equip you for battle, though you have not known Me” (Isaiah 45:5).

Scripture also holds rulers to account for justice, and Gallio's careless silence while a man was beaten falls short of it: “Defend the cause of the weak and fatherless; uphold the rights of the afflicted and oppressed” (Psalm 82:3).
passages.asks: God kept his promise to Paul through an official who did not care about God at all. Ask whether you can trust God to work through people and systems that do not share your faith. And notice Gallio's shrug while a man was beaten. Ask when you have looked away from someone being hurt because it was not your concern.

passages.t: A vow at Cenchrea, and back to Antioch
passages.happening:
Paul stays in Corinth for some time, then says goodbye. “He had his head shaved in Cenchrea to keep a vow he had made” (verse 18), and sails for Syria with Priscilla and Aquila.

At Ephesus he leaves them, goes into the synagogue and reasons with the Jews there (verse 19). They ask him to stay longer, but he declines (verse 20). As he leaves he says, “I will come back to you if God is willing” (verse 21), and sails from Ephesus.

He lands at Caesarea, goes up and greets the church in Jerusalem, then goes down to Antioch (verse 22). After some time there, he travels from place to place through Galatia and Phrygia, strengthening all the disciples (verse 23).
passages.hearers:
Cenchrea was Corinth's eastern harbour, where a church later met; Paul names Phoebe as serving the church there (Romans 16:1).

Paul's vow is one of the most Jewish moments in Acts. A vow was a promise made to God, often for a set time, perhaps in thanks or in a time of need. Luke does not tell us what Paul's vow was about. Many think it was like the Nazirite vow of the Law, in which a person set apart to God let his hair grow and then cut it at the end. Others point out that the Law asked a Nazirite to shave his head at the sanctuary and burn the hair, and think this was a private vow of a similar kind. Either way, Paul the apostle to the Gentiles still kept Jewish ways of devotion, freely and gladly.

In Ephesus, Paul goes straight into the synagogue, as always. Here the Jews ask him to stay. He promises to come back ‘if God is willing’, and he does (chapter 19).

Verses 22 and 23 cover a great distance in two sentences: a sea voyage to Caesarea, a visit to Jerusalem (Luke's ‘went up’ was the usual way of speaking of a trip to Jerusalem), a stay at Antioch, and then the long road north and west into Galatia. Readers usually count Paul's third trip as starting here.
passages.ot:
The Nazirite vow is set out in the Law: “For the entire period of his vow of separation, no razor shall pass over his head” (Numbers 6:5), and at the end, “the Nazirite is to shave his consecrated head, take the hair, and put it on the fire under the peace offering” (Numbers 6:18).

The Law also took vows seriously: “If a man makes a vow to the LORD or swears an oath to obligate himself by a pledge, he must not break his word” (Numbers 30:2). And ‘if God is willing’ is the humble trust of the wise: “Many plans are in a man’s heart, but the purpose of the LORD will prevail” (Proverbs 19:21).
passages.asks: Paul, who fought for Gentile freedom from the law, still kept a Jewish vow for his own devotion. Ask whether you can let other believers keep practices of devotion you do not keep, without judging them. And notice ‘if God is willing’. Ask how firmly you hold your own plans.

passages.t: Apollos, taught by Priscilla and Aquila
passages.happening:
Meanwhile a Jew named Apollos, from Alexandria, comes to Ephesus. “He was an eloquent man, well versed in the Scriptures” (verse 24). He has been taught the way of the Lord and is “fervent in spirit”; he speaks and teaches accurately about Jesus, “though he knew only the baptism of John” (verse 25).

He begins to speak boldly in the synagogue. “When Priscilla and Aquila heard him, they took him in and explained to him the way of God more accurately” (verse 26).

When Apollos decides to cross over to Achaia, the believers encourage him and write to the disciples there to welcome him. On his arrival he is a great help to those who by grace had believed (verse 27), for he powerfully refutes his opponents in public debate, proving from the Scriptures that Jesus is the Christ (verse 28).
passages.hearers:
Alexandria, in Egypt, was one of the great cities of the empire, with one of the largest Jewish communities in the world. It was there that the Scriptures had been translated into Greek. Apollos was a learned Jew, a gifted speaker, and he knew his Bible well.

He knew about Jesus and taught about him accurately. But he ‘knew only the baptism of John’. John the Baptist had called people to repent and be baptized, getting ready for the one who was coming. Apollos seems to have known John's message and the story of Jesus, but not the fuller teaching about Jesus' death and rising, the gift of the Spirit and baptism in his name. The next chapter meets other disciples who knew only John's baptism (19:1-7).

Priscilla and Aquila hear him in the synagogue. They do not correct him in public. They take him aside, perhaps into their home, and explain the way of God ‘more accurately’. And a famous preacher listens to a tentmaker and his wife.

Luke names Priscilla first here, as he does in verse 18. Of the six times the two are named together in the New Testament, Priscilla comes first four times (Acts 18:18, 26; Romans 16:3; 2 Timothy 4:19). Readers explain this in different ways: that she was the more prominent in the church, or that she was of higher social standing. Luke does not say why.

Apollos goes on to Achaia, to Corinth, and helps the church greatly. Paul later wrote, “I planted the seed and Apollos watered it, but God made it grow” (1 Corinthians 3:6).

Verse 28 says Apollos refuted ‘the Jews’ in public debate. These were Jews of the synagogue in Corinth who did not believe, and Apollos, himself a Jew, argued with them from the Scriptures they shared. The note on verses 5-8 above says more.
passages.ot:
Apollos proved from the Scriptures that Jesus is the Christ, the Messiah of Israel's hope. The Law and the Prophets were his whole case.

Proverbs praises the wise man who is willing to learn more: “let the wise listen and gain instruction, and the discerning acquire wise counsel” (Proverbs 1:5). And women who spoke God's word appear in the Old Testament: Deborah, “a prophetess” who led Israel (Judges 4:4), and Huldah “the prophetess”, to whom the king's officials went to hear the LORD's word (2 Kings 22:14).
passages.hard:
Priscilla, with her husband, explained the way of God to Apollos, a man and a preacher. What does this mean for women teaching in the church? Christians who hold different views both read this verse carefully. These views are held by faithful believers, and these notes do not choose between them.

Complementarian Christians believe that men and women are equal in worth before God, and that God has given them different roles in the church and the home, with the office of pastor or elder, and teaching the gathered church with that authority, given to qualified men. They point to Paul's words, “I do not permit a woman to teach or to exercise authority over a man” (1 Timothy 2:12). Many of them read this scene as Priscilla and her husband teaching together, in private and not in the gathered church, and they gladly see in it women teaching the faith in homes, small groups and one to one. They honour Priscilla as a model.

Egalitarian Christians believe that men and women are equal in worth and that every role in the church, including pastor and teacher, is open to both, as God gifts them. They point to this scene as evidence: Priscilla, named first, taught a leading preacher the way of God, and Paul calls her and Aquila ‘my fellow workers in Christ Jesus’ (Romans 16:3), with a church meeting in their house. Many of them read 1 Timothy 2:12 as addressing a particular problem in one church at one time.

Both sides agree on much: Priscilla was a gifted and respected servant of Christ, she knew the faith well enough to correct a famous preacher, and Luke honours her for it.
passages.asks: A gifted preacher let a tentmaker couple correct him, and he became more useful, not less. Ask how you receive correction, especially from people you think of as less learned than you. And notice how Priscilla and Aquila did it: privately, kindly, and with the Scriptures. Ask whether that is how you correct others.
